newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: Irish government condemns "barbaric bomb attacks".
newsitem.headline: Irish government condemns "barbaric bomb attacks".

text.p: The Irish government condemned Monday's "barbaric bomb attacks" on Britain's Northern Ireland army headquarters and said the blasts were designed to incite wider bloodshed in the troubled province.

"This outrage, carried out without warning, is deliberately calculated to provoke further violence and bloodshed and is aimed at undermining the multi-party talks in Belfast," a government statement said.
It called on Northern Ireland's citizens "to resist attempts to plunge Northern Ireland back into an appalling cycle of violence", and extended its sympathy to those injured.

The attack on the British army base in Lisburn near Belfast wounded up to 20 people, two critically. It was the first bombing of a British security target in Northern Ireland since rival Irish Republican Army (IRA) and Protestant Loyalist guerrillas declared twin ceasefires in 1994.

Irish Prime Minister John Bruton said the attack was intended to provoke a violent backlash from Loyalist guerrillas who want Northern Ireland to remain part of Britain. But he said he believed the Loyalist ceasefire would hold firm.
"This provocation will not achieve its appalling, calculated objective," Bruton told reporters.

"I believe that the good sense and restraint, which has, despite other provocations, allowed the loyalists to stick by the political path, which is the only rational path for rational people to follow, is the way that they will go."
Bruton and British Prime Minister John Major are overseeing multi-party peace talks in Northern Ireland aimed at ending the IRA's 27-year war against British rule of the province.
But Republicans accuse Major of wrecking the peace process by insisting that the IRA ends its violence before its political wing, Sinn Fein, can be admitted to the talks.
